notes.front: In radio communications, what is baseband?
notes.back: The frequency range a message signal occupies before modulation.
notes.explanation: The term names the message itself, such as microphone audio, not a band, bandwidth or oscillator of the radio.
notes.example: Like the audio from a microphone, described by the span of frequencies it covers before any carrier is involved.
notes.evidence: E7E07 (B) What is meant by the term “baseband” in radio communications? A. The lowest frequency band that the transmitter or receiver covers B. The frequency range occupied by a message signal prior to modulation

notes.front: How is the modulation index of an FM signal defined?
notes.back: Frequency deviation divided by the frequency of the modulating signal.
notes.explanation: FM has no fixed value to compare against, so 'percent of modulation' means little; the index is the useful measure.
notes.example: Like a ratio of swing to pace: a carrier swinging 2 kHz either side with a 1 kHz tone has an index of 2.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 12, chapter 2, frequency modulation, modulation index, p. 2-12
notes.evidence: Since there is no fixed value for comparison, the term "percent of modulation" has little meaning for fm. The term MODULATION INDEX is more useful in fm modulation discussions. Modulation index is frequency deviation divided by the frequency of the modulating signal.

notes.front: How is the deviation ratio of an FM system defined?
notes.back: The maximum carrier frequency deviation divided by the highest audio modulating frequency.
notes.explanation: It is the modulation index taken at the system's limits rather than for one particular tone.
notes.example: Like the modulation index, but fixed by the system's limits: a system allowing ±4 kHz with audio up to 2 kHz has a ratio of 2.
notes.evidence: E8B09 (B) What is deviation ratio? A. The ratio of the audio modulating frequency to the center carrier frequency B. The ratio of the maximum carrier frequency deviation to the highest audio modulating frequency

notes.front: What does a pre-emphasis network do in an FM speech channel?
notes.back: It boosts the higher audio frequencies.
notes.explanation: It is the network added on the speech side; the one used in FM communications receivers is de-emphasis.
notes.example: Like turning up the treble on a hi-fi, but built into the speech channel of an FM transmitter.
notes.evidence: E7E05 (D) What is added to an FM speech channel to boost the higher audio frequencies? A. A de-emphasis network B. A harmonic enhancer C. A heterodyne enhancer D. A pre-emphasis network

notes.front: Where is de-emphasis used, and what reason does the pool give for it?
notes.back: In FM communications receivers, for compatibility with transmitters using phase modulation.
notes.explanation: It is the receiving partner of pre-emphasis, the network that boosts the higher audio frequencies in the speech channel.
notes.example: Like a matching adapter, but for audio response: it suits an FM receiver to transmitters that use phase modulation.
notes.evidence: E7E06 (A) Why is de-emphasis used in FM communications receivers? A. For compatibility with transmitters using phase modulation

notes.front: What does a frequency discriminator do in an FM receiver?
notes.back: It detects FM: it converts frequency variations into amplitude variations, which are then rectified and filtered.
notes.explanation: The Foster-Seeley type, also called the phase-shift discriminator, makes the conversion with a double-tuned RF transformer.
notes.example: Like a detector for amplitude modulation, but for frequency swings: its output grows as the signal moves further from the centre frequency.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 12, chapter 3, Foster-Seeley discriminator, p. 3-12
notes.evidence: The FOSTER-SEELEY DISCRIMINATOR is also known as the PHASE-SHIFT DISCRIMINATOR. It uses a double-tuned rf transformer to convert frequency variations in the received fm signal to amplitude variations. These amplitude variations are then rectified and filtered to provide a dc output voltage.

notes.front: What is an envelope detector?
notes.back: A diode detector that reproduces the original modulating frequencies from a signal's modulation envelope.
notes.explanation: The modulation envelope approximates the original modulating waveform, so following it recovers the audio.
notes.example: Like tracing the outline of a waveform's peaks, as a simple diode receiver with headphones does.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 12, chapter 3, diode detectors, p. 3-6
notes.evidence: The vector addition of these frequencies provides the modulation envelope which approximates the original modulating waveform. It is this modulation envelope that the DIODE DETECTORS use to reproduce the original modulating frequencies.

notes.front: How does frequency division multiplexing (FDM) let several channels share one transmitter?
notes.back: Each channel occupies its own band of frequencies, and the composite signal modulates the carrier.
notes.explanation: Separating the channels by frequency is what lets them be carried together on a single carrier.
notes.example: Like several stations sharing one band, but all riding on a single transmitter's carrier as one composite signal.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 17, chapter 3, frequency division, p. 3-33
notes.evidence: Each separate channel occupies its own band of frequencies. The composite signal is used to modulate the carrier frequency of the transmitter.

notes.front: How does time division multiplexing (TDM) combine several signals?
notes.back: It samples each signal in turn; synchronised switches at each end keep every channel's samples in its own slot.
notes.explanation: With the transmitter and receiver switches synchronised, samples from transmitter channel one reach receiver channel one, and so on.
notes.example: Like people taking turns at one microphone in a fixed rota.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 17, chapter 3, time division, p. 3-32
notes.evidence: When the transmitter and receiver switches are synchronized, the signals will be fed in the proper sequence to the receiver channels. The samples from transmitter channel one will be fed to receiver channel one.

notes.front: What kind of technique is orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM)?
notes.back: A digital modulation technique using subcarriers at frequencies chosen to avoid intersymbol interference.
notes.explanation: As the name says, it divides the signal by frequency: the data is carried on subcarriers rather than one carrier.
notes.example: Like FDM, but inside one digital signal: its data rides on several subcarriers at once.
notes.evidence: What describes orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM)? A. A frequency modulation technique that uses non-harmonically related frequencies B. A bandwidth compression technique using Fourier transforms C. A digital mode for narrow-band, slow-speed transmissions D. A digital modulation technique using subcarriers at frequencies chosen to avoid intersymbol interference

notes.front: What problem are an OFDM signal's subcarrier frequencies chosen to avoid?
notes.back: Intersymbol interference.
notes.explanation: The pool defines OFDM by this choice: a digital modulation technique whose subcarriers sit at frequencies picked for the purpose.
notes.example: Like words blurring together when someone talks too fast, but between successive symbols of a data signal.
notes.evidence: D. A digital modulation technique using subcarriers at frequencies chosen to avoid intersymbol interference

notes.front: In a reactance modulator, what controls how far the oscillator's frequency moves?
notes.back: The instantaneous amplitude of the modulating voltage: the frequency changes in proportion to it.
notes.explanation: The audio varies the reactance across the oscillator, and that reactance sets the oscillator's instantaneous frequency.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 12, chapter 2, reactance-tube modulator, p. 2-17
notes.evidence: This action varies the reactance across the oscillator which, in turn, varies the instantaneous frequency of the oscillator. These variations in the oscillator frequency are proportional to the instantaneous amplitude of the modulating voltage.

notes.front: Reactance modulators are usually operated at {{c1::low}} power levels, with the output power developed in amplifier stages that follow.
notes.back: low
notes.explanation: So FM is made at the oscillator, and the power amplifier stages after the modulator build up the output.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 12, chapter 2, reactance-tube modulator, p. 2-17
notes.evidence: Reactance-tube modulators are usually operated at low power levels. The required output power is developed in power amplifier stages that follow the modulators.

notes.front: In a varactor FM modulator, what varies the varactor's capacitance?
notes.back: The reverse bias, which controls the thickness of the depletion region.
notes.explanation: The varactor is designed so that its change in capacitance is linear with the change in applied voltage.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 12, chapter 2, varactor FM modulator, p. 2-20
notes.evidence: Capacitance is varied in the varactor by varying the reverse bias which controls the thickness of the depletion region. The varactor is so designed that the change in capacitance is linear with the change in the applied voltage.

notes.front: Why is a limiter needed before a Foster-Seeley discriminator?
notes.back: Its output responds to some extent to input amplitude as well as frequency.
notes.explanation: Without limiting, amplitude variations on the input would affect the output along with the frequency variations.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 12, chapter 3, Foster-Seeley discriminator, p. 3-12
notes.evidence: The output of the Foster-Seeley discriminator is affected not only by the input frequency, but also to a certain extent by the input amplitude. Therefore, using limiter stages before the detector is necessary.

notes.front: What two conditions must a circuit meet for mixing (heterodyning) to occur?
notes.back: At least two different frequencies must be applied, and they must be applied to a nonlinear impedance.
notes.explanation: Together these produce the new sum and difference frequencies that a mixer is used for.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 12, chapter 1, typical heterodyning circuit, p. 1-25
notes.evidence: Two conditions must be met in a circuit for heterodyning to occur. First, at least two different frequencies must be applied to the circuit. Second, these signals must be applied to a nonlinear impedance. These two conditions will result in new frequencies (sum and difference) being produced.

notes.front: In the Navy receiver with three demodulators, which signals does the product detector handle?
notes.back: SSB, CW and FSK signals.
notes.explanation: The receiver's other two detectors are dedicated: one demodulates amplitude-modulated signals, the other FM signals only.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 17, chapter 5, receiver demodulators, p. 5-7
notes.evidence: They are the AM detector, product detector, and fm detector. The AM detector is used to demodulate AM signals. The product detector demodulates ssb, cw, and fsk signals, and the fm detector demodulates fm signals only.

notes.front: What must an SSB receiver supply that the received signal lacks?
notes.back: A carrier of the proper frequency and amplitude, reinserted at the receiver.
notes.explanation: The sidebands bear a direct relationship to the carrier, so they cannot be demodulated properly without it.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 17, chapter 2, single-sideband receiver, p. 2-15
notes.evidence: Also, a carrier of proper frequency and amplitude must be reinserted at the receiver because of the direct relationship between the carrier and sidebands.

notes.front: In a series-diode detector, what do the diode and its bypass capacitor each do?
notes.back: The diode conducts one way, removing the negative half of the RF carrier; the capacitor filters (smooths) what remains.
notes.explanation: That is rectification followed by filtering, which is how the pool describes a diode envelope detector.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 12, chapter 3, series-diode detector, p. 3-7
notes.evidence: Because the semiconductor is a nonlinear device, it conducts in only one direction. This eliminates the negative portion of the rf carrier and produces the signal shown in view (C). The current in the circuit must be smoothed before the headphones can reproduce the af intelligence. This action is achieved by C2 which acts as a filter to

notes.front: What does an FM signal's modulation index tell you about its spectrum?
notes.back: The number of significant sidebands; with the modulating frequency, that sets the bandwidth.
notes.explanation: In the Navy table an index of 1.0 gives 6 significant sidebands and an index of 5.0 gives 16.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 12, chapter 2, summary, p. 2-55
notes.evidence: The number of SIGNIFICANT SIDEBANDS and the modulating frequency will determine the bandwidth of the fm wave. The number of significant sidebands can be determined from the modulation index. MODULATION SIGNIFICANT INDEX SIDEBANDS .01 2 .4 2 .5 4 1.0 6 2.0 8 3.0 12 4.0 14 5.0 16

notes.front: How often must each audio channel be sampled in a time-division system?
notes.back: At least twice per cycle of audio; practical systems usually take about 2.4 samples per cycle.
notes.explanation: More samples are allowed, but fewer than two per cycle does not give satisfactory results.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 17, chapter 3, time division, p. 3-30
notes.evidence: no limit to the maximum number of samples that may be made, but you must sample at least twice per cycle of audio to get satisfactory results. In practical systems, 2.4 samples per cycle are usually taken.

notes.front: Which of the following can be used to generate FM phone signals?
notes.choices:
A) Balanced modulation of the audio amplifier
B) Reactance modulation of a local oscillator
C) Reactance modulation of the final amplifier
D) Balanced modulation of a local oscillator
notes.back: Reactance modulation of a local oscillator
notes.choicesExplained: A and D: balanced modulation is the first step in making SSB, not FM. C: reactance modulators are usually run at low power; output power comes from the amplifier stages that follow.
notes.explanation: Reactance modulation varies the reactance across an oscillator, which varies its instantaneous frequency: frequency modulation, made at low power.
notes.evidence: Which of the following can be used to generate FM phone signals?

notes.front: What is the function of a reactance modulator?
notes.choices:
A) Produce PM or FM signals by varying a resistance
B) Produce AM signals by varying an inductance
C) Produce AM signals by varying a resistance
D) Produce PM or FM signals by varying a capacitance
notes.back: Produce PM or FM signals by varying a capacitance
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: the modulator varies a reactance across the oscillator, not a resistance. B and C: changing the oscillator's reactance changes its frequency or phase, not its amplitude.
notes.explanation: The modulating voltage varies the reactance across the oscillator; in a varactor modulator the reverse bias sets the capacitance, and so the frequency.
notes.evidence: What is the function of a reactance modulator?

notes.front: What is a frequency discriminator?
notes.choices:
A) An FM generator circuit
B) A circuit for filtering closely adjacent signals
C) An automatic band-switching circuit
D) A circuit for detecting FM signals
notes.back: A circuit for detecting FM signals
notes.choicesExplained: A: FM is generated by a modulator, such as a reactance modulator. B: separating closely spaced signals is a filter's job. C: band switching has nothing to do with detection.
notes.explanation: A discriminator converts the received signal's frequency variations into amplitude variations, which are then rectified and filtered into the output.
notes.evidence: What is a frequency discriminator?

notes.front: What is one way to produce a single-sideband phone signal?
notes.choices:
A) Use a balanced modulator followed by a filter
B) Use a reactance modulator followed by a mixer
C) Use a loop modulator followed by a mixer
D) Use a product detector with a DSB signal
notes.back: Use a balanced modulator followed by a filter
notes.choicesExplained: B: a reactance modulator produces FM or PM. C: 'loop modulator' is a distractor. D: a product detector demodulates SSB in a receiver; it does not generate it.
notes.explanation: A balanced modulator gives double sideband with the carrier suppressed; the filter then leaves just one sideband.
notes.evidence: What is one way to produce a single-sideband phone signal?

notes.front: What is added to an FM speech channel to boost the higher audio frequencies?
notes.choices:
A) A de-emphasis network
B) A harmonic enhancer
C) A heterodyne enhancer
D) A pre-emphasis network
notes.back: A pre-emphasis network
notes.choicesExplained: A: de-emphasis is the receiver's network, not the one that boosts the highs. B and C: harmonic and heterodyne 'enhancers' are distractors.
notes.explanation: The boost is applied to the speech audio; the receiver's matching network is de-emphasis.
notes.evidence: What is added to an FM speech channel to boost the higher audio frequencies?

notes.front: Why is de-emphasis used in FM communications receivers?
notes.choices:
A) For compatibility with transmitters using phase modulation
B) To reduce impulse noise reception
C) For higher efficiency
D) To remove third-order distortion products
notes.back: For compatibility with transmitters using phase modulation
notes.choicesExplained: B: the stated reason is compatibility with PM transmitters, not impulse noise. C: efficiency is not what it is for. D: it is not a way of removing distortion products.
notes.explanation: A phase modulator’s deviation rises with audio frequency, as if pre-emphasis were built in; de-emphasis in the receiver cuts the highs back, so FM receivers work with PM transmitters.
notes.evidence: Why is de-emphasis used in FM communications receivers?

notes.front: What is meant by the term “baseband” in radio communications?
notes.choices:
A) The lowest frequency band that the transmitter or receiver covers
B) The frequency range occupied by a message signal prior to modulation
C) The unmodulated bandwidth of the transmitted signal
D) The basic oscillator frequency in an FM transmitter that is multiplied to increase the deviation and carrier frequency
notes.back: The frequency range occupied by a message signal prior to modulation
notes.choicesExplained: A: that describes a radio's lowest band, not the message. C: the transmitted signal's bandwidth exists only after modulation. D: that describes a frequency-multiplied FM oscillator, not the message.
notes.explanation: Baseband describes the message itself, such as speech audio, before any carrier is involved.
notes.evidence: What is meant by the term “baseband” in radio communications?

notes.front: What are the principal frequencies that appear at the output of a mixer?
notes.choices:
A) Two and four times the input frequency
B) The square root of the product of input frequencies
C) The two input frequencies along with their sum and difference frequencies
D) 1.414 and 0.707 times the input frequency
notes.back: The two input frequencies along with their sum and difference frequencies
notes.choicesExplained: A: multiples of one frequency are harmonics, not mixer products. B: the square root of the product is not a mixing product. D: 1.414 and 0.707 are voltage ratios, not mixer frequencies.
notes.explanation: Two different frequencies applied to a nonlinear impedance produce new sum and difference frequencies alongside the originals.
notes.evidence: What are the principal frequencies that appear at the output of a mixer?

notes.front: What occurs when the input signal levels to a mixer are too high?
notes.choices:
A) Spurious mixer products are generated
B) Mixer blanking occurs
C) Automatic limiting occurs
D) Excessive AGC voltage levels are generated
notes.back: Spurious mixer products are generated
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: neither blanking nor limiting is how a mixer responds to overload. D: AGC voltage comes from the receiver's gain-control circuit, not from mixer overload.
notes.explanation: Driven too hard, a mixer becomes even more nonlinear, so harmonics of its inputs mix as well, adding spurious products beside the wanted sum and difference.
notes.evidence: What occurs when the input signal levels to a mixer are too high?

notes.front: How does a diode envelope detector function?
notes.choices:
A) By rectification and filtering of RF signals
B) By breakdown of the Zener voltage
C) By mixing signals with noise in the transition region of the diode
D) By sensing the change of reactance in the diode with respect to frequency
notes.back: By rectification and filtering of RF signals
notes.choicesExplained: B: Zener breakdown is used for voltage regulation, not detection. C: mixing with noise plays no part. D: a change of diode reactance with frequency plays no part either.
notes.explanation: The diode conducts in one direction only, removing half of the RF carrier, and a capacitor smooths the result into audio.
notes.evidence: How does a diode envelope detector function?

notes.front: Which type of detector is used for demodulating SSB signals?
notes.choices:
A) Discriminator
B) Phase detector
C) Product detector
D) Phase comparator
notes.back: Product detector
notes.choicesExplained: A: a discriminator detects FM. B and D: these compare phases rather than recovering SSB audio.
notes.explanation: An SSB receiver must reinsert a carrier of proper frequency and amplitude; the product detector demodulates SSB, CW and FSK signals.
notes.evidence: Which type of detector is used for demodulating SSB signals?

notes.front: What is the modulation index of an FM signal?
notes.choices:
A) The ratio of frequency deviation to modulating signal frequency
B) The ratio of modulating signal amplitude to frequency deviation
C) The modulating signal frequency divided by the bandwidth of the transmitted signal
D) The bandwidth of the transmitted signal divided by the modulating signal frequency
notes.back: The ratio of frequency deviation to modulating signal frequency
notes.choicesExplained: B: that inverts the ratio and uses amplitude instead of frequency. C and D: bandwidth follows from the index; it is not part of its definition.
notes.explanation: Deviation and modulating frequency together set the number and spacing of the side frequencies, so the index is the useful FM measure.
notes.evidence: What is the modulation index of an FM signal?

notes.front: How does the modulation index of a phase-modulated emission vary with RF carrier frequency?
notes.choices:
A) It increases as the RF carrier frequency increases
B) It decreases as the RF carrier frequency increases
C) It varies with the square root of the RF carrier frequency
D) It does not depend on the RF carrier frequency
notes.back: It does not depend on the RF carrier frequency
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: each ties the index to the carrier frequency, which does not enter into it.
notes.explanation: In PM the amount of phase shift follows the modulating signal's amplitude and its rate follows the modulating frequency; the carrier frequency is not a factor.
notes.evidence: How does the modulation index of a phase-modulated emission vary with RF carrier frequency?

notes.front: What is the modulation index of an FM phone signal having a maximum frequency deviation of 3000 Hz either side of the carrier frequency if the highest modulating frequency is 1000 Hz?
notes.choicesExplained: B and D: fractions would need less deviation than audio frequency. C: 6 counts the swing on both sides of the carrier; use the deviation either side.
notes.explanation: Divide the deviation by the modulating frequency: 3,000 Hz ÷ 1,000 Hz = 3.
notes.evidence: What is the modulation index of an FM phone signal having a maximum frequency deviation of 3000 Hz either side of the carrier frequency if the highest modulating frequency is 1000 Hz?

notes.front: What is the modulation index of an FM phone signal having a maximum carrier deviation of plus or minus 6 kHz if the highest modulating frequency is 2 kHz?
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: fractions would need less deviation than audio frequency. D: 6 is the deviation itself, not divided by the audio frequency.
notes.explanation: Take the deviation on one side of the carrier: 6 kHz ÷ 2 kHz = 3.
notes.evidence: What is the modulation index of an FM phone signal having a maximum carrier deviation of plus or minus 6 kHz if the highest modulating frequency is 2 kHz?

notes.front: What is the deviation ratio of an FM phone signal having a maximum frequency swing of plus or minus 5 kHz if the highest modulation frequency is 3 kHz?
notes.choicesExplained: A: 6 is not 5 ÷ 3. B: 0.167 misplaces the decimal point. C: 0.6 is the ratio inverted (3 ÷ 5).
notes.explanation: Maximum deviation over highest modulating frequency: 5 kHz ÷ 3 kHz = 1.67.
notes.evidence: What is the deviation ratio of an FM phone signal having a maximum frequency swing of plus or minus 5 kHz if the highest modulation frequency is 3 kHz?

notes.front: What is the deviation ratio of an FM phone signal having a maximum frequency swing of plus or minus 7.5 kHz if the highest modulation frequency is 3.5 kHz?
notes.choicesExplained: B: 0.214 misplaces the decimal point. C: 0.47 is the ratio inverted (3.5 ÷ 7.5). D: 47 is not a ratio of these numbers.
notes.explanation: Maximum deviation over highest modulating frequency: 7.5 kHz ÷ 3.5 kHz = 2.14.
notes.evidence: What is the deviation ratio of an FM phone signal having a maximum frequency swing of plus or minus 7.5 kHz if the highest modulation frequency is 3.5 kHz?

notes.front: Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) is a technique used for which types of amateur communication?
notes.choices:
A) Digital modes
B) Extremely low-power contacts
C) EME
D) OFDM signals are not allowed on amateur bands
notes.back: Digital modes
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing ties it to low-power contacts. C: EME names a path to the Moon and back, not a modulation. D: the pool places it among amateur digital modes.
notes.explanation: OFDM is a digital modulation technique, carrying data on subcarriers, so it belongs with the digital modes.
notes.evidence: Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) is a technique used for which types of amateur communication?

notes.front: What describes orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM)?
notes.choices:
A) A frequency modulation technique that uses non-harmonically related frequencies
B) A bandwidth compression technique using Fourier transforms
C) A digital mode for narrow-band, slow-speed transmissions
D) A digital modulation technique using subcarriers at frequencies chosen to avoid intersymbol interference
notes.back: A digital modulation technique using subcarriers at frequencies chosen to avoid intersymbol interference
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is not FM on non-harmonic frequencies. B: its purpose is not bandwidth compression. C: it is not defined as a narrow, slow-speed mode.
notes.explanation: Its data rides on subcarriers whose frequencies are chosen to avoid intersymbol interference; it is a modulation technique, not compression.
notes.evidence: What describes orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM)?

notes.front: What is deviation ratio?
notes.choices:
A) The ratio of the audio modulating frequency to the center carrier frequency
B) The ratio of the maximum carrier frequency deviation to the highest audio modulating frequency
C) The ratio of the carrier center frequency to the audio modulating frequency
D) The ratio of the highest audio modulating frequency to the average audio modulating frequency
notes.back: The ratio of the maximum carrier frequency deviation to the highest audio modulating frequency
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: the carrier frequency is not part of the ratio. D: average audio frequency plays no part.
notes.explanation: It is the modulation index taken at the system's limits: the largest deviation over the highest audio frequency.
notes.evidence: What is deviation ratio?

notes.front: What is frequency division multiplexing (FDM)?
notes.choices:
A) The transmitted signal jumps from band to band at a predetermined rate
B) Dividing the transmitted signal into separate frequency bands that each carry a different data stream
C) The transmitted signal is divided into packets of information
D) Two or more information streams are merged into a digital combiner, which then pulse position modulates the transmitter
notes.back: Dividing the transmitted signal into separate frequency bands that each carry a different data stream
notes.choicesExplained: A: jumping from band to band describes frequency hopping. C: dividing into packets is packet transmission. D: pulse-position modulation through a digital combiner is not frequency division.
notes.explanation: Each channel occupies its own band of frequencies, and the composite signal modulates the carrier.
notes.evidence: What is frequency division multiplexing (FDM)?

notes.front: What is digital time division multiplexing?
notes.choices:
A) Two or more data streams are assigned to discrete sub-carriers on an FM transmitter
B) Two or more signals are arranged to share discrete time slots of a data transmission
C) Two or more data streams share the same channel by transmitting time of transmission as the sub-carrier
D) Two or more signals are quadrature modulated to increase bandwidth efficiency
notes.back: Two or more signals are arranged to share discrete time slots of a data transmission
notes.choicesExplained: A: separate sub-carriers is frequency division. C: transmitting time as a sub-carrier is not a multiplexing method. D: quadrature modulation is a different technique, not time sharing.
notes.explanation: Each signal is sampled periodically, and synchronised switching keeps each channel's samples in its own place in the chain.
notes.evidence: What is digital time division multiplexing?

notes.front: A 2-metre FM transmitter swings 2.5 kHz either side of its carrier when modulated by a 500 Hz test tone. What is the modulation index?
notes.choicesExplained: A: 0.2 is the tone divided by the deviation, the ratio upside down. C: 3 would need 1.5 kHz of deviation with this tone. D: 2,500 is the deviation in hertz, not a ratio.
notes.explanation: Divide the deviation by the modulating frequency: 2,500 Hz ÷ 500 Hz = 5.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 12, chapter 2, frequency modulation, modulation index, p. 2-12
notes.evidence: The term MODULATION INDEX is more useful in fm modulation discussions. Modulation index is frequency deviation divided by the frequency of the modulating signal.

notes.front: An FM voice system allows at most ±4.5 kHz of deviation and passes audio up to 3 kHz. What is its deviation ratio?
notes.choicesExplained: A: 0.67 divides the audio by the deviation, the ratio inverted. C: 7.5 adds the two figures. D: 13.5 multiplies them.
notes.explanation: Deviation ratio is the maximum deviation over the highest audio frequency: 4.5 kHz ÷ 3 kHz = 1.5.
notes.evidence: B. The ratio of the maximum carrier frequency deviation to the highest audio modulating frequency

notes.front: A receiver has three detectors: one for amplitude modulation, a product detector and one for FM. You retune from an FM signal to a CW signal. Which detector now does the work?
notes.choices:
A) The amplitude-modulation detector
B) The product detector
C) The FM detector
D) None: CW needs no detector
notes.back: The product detector
notes.choicesExplained: A: that detector handles amplitude-modulated signals. C: the FM detector demodulates FM signals only. D: CW still has to be demodulated, and here the product detector does it.
notes.explanation: In the Navy receiver described, the product detector demodulates SSB, CW and FSK signals.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 17, chapter 5, receiver demodulators, p. 5-7
notes.evidence: The product detector demodulates ssb, cw, and fsk signals, and the fm detector demodulates fm signals only.

notes.front: How does an FM signal's modulation index differ from a system's deviation ratio?
notes.back: The index uses the actual deviation and modulating frequency; the deviation ratio uses the maximum deviation and the highest audio frequency.
notes.explanation: So a system has one deviation ratio, while the index changes with each tone's frequency and level.
notes.evidence: E8B09 (B) What is deviation ratio? A. The ratio of the audio modulating frequency to the center carrier frequency B. The ratio of the maximum carrier frequency deviation to the highest audio modulating frequency

notes.front: How do FDM and TDM differ in what they send of each signal?
notes.back: FDM sends the whole of every signal, each in its own frequency band; TDM sends periodic samples of each signal in turn.
notes.explanation: Frequency division transmits and receives the full 360 degrees of each sine wave, whereas time division only samples each signal periodically.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 17, chapter 3, summary, p. 3-45
notes.evidence: TIME-DIVISION multiplexing is the process that periodically samples several intelligence signals. This can be a received signal or one to be transmitted. FREQUENCY-DIVISION multiplexing transmits and receives the full 360 degrees of each sine wave.
